title: APIS India — Risk & Reputation Research
content:
The sources indicate that Apis Services Inc. has received negative reviews regarding its management and work environment, with one review on Indeed.com stating, "This is the most toxic company I have ever worked for. Management does not care about the hard working employees at all and are more interested in scolding them than assisting them." Another review mentions, "Company does not retain staff. From supervisors to attendants keep leaving the job. No incentive for staff." However, the sources do not provide specific information on customer complaints and negative reviews for APIS India's products.

Apis products may be available on the brand's official website and authorised marketplaces including Amazon and Flipkart. Counterfeit food and supplement products are a known problem in India, so always purchase from verified channels and reputed sellers. Avoid third-party resellers or unverified sellers, as product authenticity cannot be guaranteed outside authorised sources. [...] We bought every Apis product from the open market, with no brand involvement. Each Apis product was third-party tested at up to 3 NABL-accredited, FSSAI-approved labs and rated D to A+ on their label accuracy, toxicity and nutrition profile (for foods).

Apis had no influence on the product ratings. All ratings stay valid for only 12 months, and all lab reports are published on Apis’s product pages.

The sources indicate that there is a legal dispute involving APIS India (ANI) and OpenAI regarding alleged infringement of copyrighted works. The court in India rejected ANI's application for an interim injunction, focusing on the training of OpenAI's LLM and the reproduction in its outputs. The court determined it had jurisdiction over the case despite the training occurring outside India. The sources do not provide a definitive answer regarding the final outcome of the action.

Court has issued an important decision in this case brought by ANI, one of India's largest news agencies, against OpenAI, rejecting ANI's application for an interim injunction pending trial. This is the first decision from India on issues of infringement in both inputs and outputs but, as an interim decision, it has no bearing on the final outcome of the action. A number of intervenors made arguments before the Court, in support of both ANI and OpenAI. The sources indicate that APIS India D2C brands face significant reputation problems and criticism primarily due to trust issues. The sources highlight that counterfeit and quality concerns are prevalent in India, especially in categories like beauty, supplements, and electronics, where counterfeit products are a known problem. D2C brands in these categories need to invest more deliberately in authenticity signals to build trust. The sources also mention that high website traffic with low conversion rates, strong social media engagement that does not translate into sales, and cart abandonment at the payment stage are specific, measurable ways trust failures manifest. The sources don't provide a definitive answer to APIS India D2C's specific reputation problems and criticism.

This is the central structural challenge of every direct-to-consumer brand operating in India. And it is also why so many D2C brands that have built genuinely good products still struggle to grow past a certain point — not because the product is wrong, but because trust, at scale, has not been engineered as deliberately as the product was. [...] This hesitation shows up in specific, measurable ways. High website traffic with low conversion rates. Strong social media engagement that does not translate into sales. Cart abandonment at the payment stage. Consumers who add a product, research it further, and never return. Each of these is a trust failure, not an awareness failure — the consumer found the brand, was interested enough to consider it, and then could not get comfortable enough to complete the purchase. [...] Counterfeit and quality concerns are more present in the Indian consumer’s mind than in many other markets, particularly in categories like beauty, supplements, and electronics where counterfeit products are a known and widely discussed problem. D2C brands in these categories need to invest more deliberately in authenticity signals — batch verification, manufacturing transparency, ingredient sourcing detail — than the same category might require in a market with less counterfeit prevalence.
